1.pericope_label: Mordecai’s bitter cry, the gate that bars sackcloth, and the raiment Esther sends in vain

schools.summary: Gill allows that Mordecai learned of the decree by common fame or on sight of the edicts published in Shushan, while recording that the Jews think it was made known supernaturally, the former Targum saying by Elijah and the latter by the Holy Ghost. Of the provinces he keeps to the reach of the thing, that the day was fixed for every place where Jews were to be found. Of the maids and chamberlains he supposes they may have told the queen merely as a piece of news, there being something shocking in it to tender minds, or told her nothing more than that Mordecai was in sackcloth, having observed by some incident that she had a peculiar respect for him.

Clarke says Mordecai gave every demonstration of poignant and oppressive grief, nor did he hide it from the city, and reports from the Greek that he protested aloud that a people were going to be destroyed who had done no evil. Of the universal silence he is blunt: how astonishing that in all this there is not the slightest intimation given of praying to God. He explains the gate by the law, that Mordecai could not enter the place where the officers waited while he was in a mourner’s habit; and of the raiment he supposes the queen thought he must somehow have been spoiled of his clothes, and so sent him clothing.

Henry sees deliberate publicity in the mourning: Mordecai not only vented his grief but proclaimed it, that all might notice he was not ashamed to own himself a friend to the Jews and a fellow-sufferer with them, however despicable Haman’s faction now made them; it was nobly done to espouse publicly a cause he knew to be righteous when it seemed a sinking one, and he laid the danger to heart more than any because Haman’s spite was against him primarily. Of the court he observes that nothing but what was gay and pleasant might appear there, the king being unwilling to hear such complaints, and that to forbid sackcloth to enter unless they could forbid sickness and trouble and death to enter was a jest. Of the provinces he counts the cost in ordinary comforts, the tables and the beds denied; and of the refused raiment he says she sent the oil of joy for mourning and the garments of praise for the spirit of heaviness, but Mordecai would make her sensible of the greatness of his grief, and so of its cause.

Ellicott observes that the sorrow of Mordecai and of the Jews alike is described by external manifestations solely, with nothing said of prayer and entreaty to the God of Israel, and sets Daniel and Ezra and Nehemiah against them as Jews who likewise submitted to the rule of the alien but who besought their God when danger threatened, and not in vain; of the gate he supplies the motive, that nothing sad or ill-omened might meet the monarch’s gaze, as though by shutting his eyes to sorrow or sickness or death he might suppose he was evading them; and from the messengers he thinks it perhaps fair to infer that Esther’s connection with Mordecai was known to those about her, though not yet to the king. Keil and Delitzsch take the king’s gate to be the open space before the entrance to the royal palace, read the prohibition as an impersonal construction, there is no entering, parse the clause naming the place in the next verse as an adverbial accusative in apposition, explain the spreading of sackcloth and ashes as many sitting in hairy garments upon the earth where ashes had been spread, and judge that the raiment was sent evidently to enable Mordecai to enter the palace and give the queen the particulars, her own distress being named by an intensive form.

debates.question: Why did Esther send raiment to Mordecai?

positions.view: She supposed he had somehow been spoiled of his clothes, and sent him replacements
To put him in a state to enter the palace and tell her what had happened
As comfort offered and refused, that she might be made to feel the greatness of his grief

outliers.claim: Alone in marshalling Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah as men under the same alien rule who did pray, so making the silence here a reproach rather than an omission.
Alone in reporting the Targums’ supernatural notice to Mordecai, by Elijah or by the Holy Ghost, while himself preferring common fame or the published edicts.

themes: Mordecai rent his clothes, and put on sackcloth with ashes, and cried with a loud and a bitter cry
none might enter into the king’s gate clothed with sackcloth
in every province, whithersoever the king’s commandment and his decree came, there was great mourning among the Jews
she sent raiment to clothe Mordecai, and to take away his sackcloth from him: but he received it not

5.pericope_label: Hatach carries the question, and brings back the sum, the copy of the decree, and the charge

schools.summary: Henry explains why the whole exchange had to go through a servant: so strictly did the laws of Persia confine the king’s wives that it was not possible for Mordecai to have a conference with Esther at all, and Hatach, whom the king had appointed to attend her, seems to have been one she could confide in. Her enquiry he turns into a rule, that to enquire after news, so that we may know the better how to direct our griefs and joys, our prayers and praises, well becomes all that love Sion, for if we must weep with those that weep we must know why they weep. Of the copy he says she must see the danger she and her people were in; and of the charge, that if she had any respect for him or kindness for the Jewish nation she should appear now on their behalf, rectify the misinformations by which the king had been imposed upon, and set the matter in a true light, not doubting that he would then vacate the decree.

Clarke reads the eunuch’s appointment without charity: he was set to wait upon the queen partly, as is still the case in the East, to serve her, and partly to observe her conduct, for no despot is exempt from a twofold torture, jealousy and suspicion. On the charge to go in to the king he reports that the Greek inserts a plea in Mordecai’s own mouth, bidding her remember the time of her low estate and how she had been nourished and carried in his arms, and pray to the Lord and plead with the king for deliverance from death, but observes that there is not a word of this in the Hebrew, the Syriac, or the Vulgate.

Gill notes that the Targum makes this officer Daniel, but thinks it not likely Daniel lived so long, and settles for the double fact that the king trusted him with the queen’s care and that she herself had a high opinion of him. He observes that Mordecai was in the street in a public manner, expressing his grief; fixes the grievance behind the report, that for refusing to reverence Haman he was incensed against Mordecai and against all the Jews for his sake, and had vowed revenge and formed a scheme for their ruin; and explains how the copy came to hand, the decree having been published in the city, so Mordecai had sight of it and transcribed it.

Keil and Delitzsch render the queen’s commission with the bluntness of the Hebrew, to learn what this and why this, that is, the meaning and the cause of his thus going about in mourning, and place the interview in the open place of the city before the king’s gate. They make the money the chief point of the report, the amount Haman had promised to weigh to the king’s treasures, that is, to pay into the royal treasury, for leave to destroy the Jews, the term being properly a determined and accurate statement and hence a sum. On the following infinitives they take them forward rather than back, with Bertheau, so that what must be supplied is that Mordecai commissioned Hatach to declare the matter to Esther and command her to go in unto the king. Ellicott adds only that the word rendered street means the square or wide open place.

debates.question: What is the heart of what Mordecai reported?

positions.view: The money Haman promised to pay into the treasury, mentioned emphatically as the chief point
The personal grievance over the refused reverence, from which the scheme grew
The danger to Esther and her people, which the copy was sent to make plain

outliers.claim: Alone in quoting the plea the Greek puts in Mordecai’s mouth here, and alone in noting that the Hebrew, the Syriac and the Vulgate have not a word of it.
Alone in weighing and rejecting the Targum’s identification of Hatach with Daniel on grounds of chronology.

themes: Then called Esther for Hatach, one of the king’s chamberlains, whom he had appointed to attend upon her
to know what it was, and why it was
the sum of the money that Haman had promised to pay to the king’s treasuries for the Jews, to destroy them
he gave him the copy of the writing of the decree that was given at Shushan
to charge her that she should go in unto the king, to make supplication unto him

10.pericope_label: The law of the inner court, and Mordecai’s answer: who knoweth whether thou art come for such a time as this

schools.summary: Clarke traces the law to pretension: the Persian sovereigns affected the highest degree of majesty, even to assuming Divine honours, so that none dared appear unveiled before them without hazarding life, and into the inner chamber of the harem none entered but the king and the woman he had chosen to call thither. On the thirty days he suspects a hand, and cannot but think Haman the cause, having endeavoured to draw the king’s attention from the queen so that his affection might be lessened. The famous question he expands into a challenge: is it likely Divine providence would have so distinguished her, raising her from abject obscurity, merely for her own sake, and has he not put her where she may counteract the most ruinous purpose ever formed? and he makes it general, that no human being lacks some particular station, by an especial providence and at some particular time, in which he may be of essential service to his neighbour. Wesley allows a reason of state, that the law was decreed to maintain the majesty and the safety of the king’s person, but adds the contrivance of the greater officers, that few might have access to the king but themselves and their friends; he says the thirty days gave her just cause to fear the king’s affections were alienated, and draws the lesson that we should consider for what end God has put us where we are, and when an opportunity offers of serving God and our generation, take care not to let it slip.

Ellicott keeps to the Hebrew, that literally one is his law, one unvarying rule for such; supports the sceptre from the monuments, the monarch in the Persian royal representations at Persepolis always holding a long staff or sceptre in his right hand; and sets the contrast forcibly between this self-styled king of kings, to enter whose presence even as a suppliant was to risk death, and the King of Kings who himself instructs man to say, let us go into his tabernacle and fall low on our knees before his footstool. He translates the hope more narrowly, enlargement being literally a breathing-space, thinks Mordecai speaks with studied reserve though we may suppose he means Divine help, and will not take the saying for proof of the man’s faith, since had his faith been like that of many of his countrymen he would not have been in Persia at all but with the struggling band in the homeland; and he finds in the whole tone of the conversation a lack of nobler feeling, no suggestion of turning for aid to God. Keil and Delitzsch press the first clause, that to be saved in the king’s house above all the Jews means saved alone of all the Jews, and render the rest without softening: recovery and deliverance will arise from another place, but thou and thy father’s house shall be destroyed.

Gill notices who knew the law: not the courtiers only but the meanest of the king’s subjects, there being scarce a person in the empire to whom it was unknown, which shows how notorious it was. Of the queen’s hesitation he keeps to the plain ground, that she would not speak to the king in favour of the Jews because of the danger she would be exposed to in doing it.

debates.question: Why was the law of the inner court made?

positions.view: Royal pretension, the Persian kings affecting majesty to the point of Divine honours
Partly the majesty and safety of the king, partly the contrivance of great officers guarding access

debates.question: Does Mordecai’s confidence that deliverance will come prove the strength of his faith?

positions.view: Yes: the language of strong faith, which God is behind, and which the event justified
No: he speaks with studied reserve, and a faith like that would not have left him in Persia at all

outliers.claim: Alone in bringing the Persepolis monuments to the golden sceptre, and alone in judging the whole exchange deficient for never turning to God.

themes: whosoever, whether man or woman, shall come unto the king into the inner court, who is not called, there is one law of his to put him to death
except such to whom the king shall hold out the golden sceptre, that he may live
but I have not been called to come in unto the king these thirty days
Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king’s house, more than all the Jews
then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place
who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?

15.pericope_label: The three days’ fast, if I perish I perish, and Mordecai goes his way

schools.summary: Wesley reads the command to fast as a command to fast and pray, as they were used to do, leaving off their common dinners by day and suppers at night and eating no more than mere necessity required, that so they might give themselves to constant and fervent prayer; the maidens he takes to be those she had chosen to attend her person, doubtless Jews or proselytes. He reckons the three days out with care, taking the qualification to belong to the time rather than the thing, and observing that the fast began at evening, so she might continue it three whole nights, two whole days and the greatest part of the third, a part of a day being reputed a day in the account of scripture and of other authors; she might have fasted all that day too, since it is probable she went not to the king till he had dined, hoping to find him in the mildest humour. Clarke refuses to supply the prayer: what a strange thing, he writes, that still we hear nothing of prayer, nor of God, and asked on what ground we can account for this total silence he answers that he does not know; she could not suppose there was any charm in fasting, in sackcloth garments, in lying on the ground, and if these were not done to turn away the displeasure of God, which seemed now to have unchained their enemies, what were they done for? Of the resolve he is warmer, that if she lose her life in this attempt to save her people she will lose it cheerfully, seeing it her duty and resolved come what will to do it, though he adds that she must have depended much on the efficacy of the humiliations she prescribed.

Gill sees a precaution in the wording of the summons: the Jews of Shushan were gathered to be acquainted with what follows, not to continue in a body together, which might cause suspicion of an ill design. He will not take the numbers he finds, either, the latter Targum reporting twelve thousand chosen priests in the city, which must be an exaggeration, since it can hardly be thought there were so many Jews there in all. On the last verse he notes that the verb used has sometimes the sense of passing over or transgressing, and reports that Jarchi took it so, of Mordecai transgressing the command by fasting on a festival, the letter having been written on the thirteenth of Nisan and the next day being the passover, on which he supposes the fast began, so that the three days fell within the feast of unleavened bread, as the Targum also has it.
Keil and Delitzsch take the last verse simply, that Mordecai went from the place before the court of the king to do what the queen had commanded.

debates.question: Did the fast Esther ordered include prayer?

positions.view: Yes: to fast is to fast and pray, as they were used to do, and the abstinence was for the sake of constant and fervent prayer
No, and the silence cannot be accounted for: still we hear nothing of prayer, nor of God

outliers.claim: Alone in reporting Jarchi’s reading of the verb as transgression, making Mordecai’s going a fast kept on the passover.
Alone in weighing and rejecting the latter Targum’s twelve thousand priests at Shushan as an exaggeration.

themes: Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me
neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise
so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law
and if I perish, I perish
So Mordecai went his way, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him
